accuracy.reason: All five objectives correctly explain interaction roles, protocol/message meanings, local-session versus stateless dependency, centralized-service costs and response uncertainty. Exact linked RFC sections, autoscaling guidance and MDN server-side source inspected live; OWASP followup supports trusted access checks.

evidence.quote: These are roles in an interaction, not types of computer.

mechanisms.reason: Cards 1-2 trace role reversal and agreed request/status fields with server checks; 3 explains what survives handler replacement by locating session state; 4 connects round trips/dependencies/overload to failure; 5 distinguishes processing from response receipt. Every objective has actors and consequences.

evidence.quote: No response leaves the outcome uncertain: processing may have failed, or processing may have succeeded and only the response was lost.

coherence.reason: All five card objectives and prerequisite edges are met. Request/response arrows, optional illustrative database, local-versus-shared-session and client/server tradeoff diagrams reinforce the surrounding text. Either stateless handler is explicitly limited to equivalent configuration and accessible required context.

evidence.quote: Moving state to shared storage helps replace handlers but leaves a storage dependency.

decisions.reason: Explains placement for shared rules versus quick/offline client work, server-side trust checks, explicit session/storage dependencies and finite capacity. Retry is a deliberate application choice because no response does not establish no effect; model names are insufficient.

evidence.quote: the client/server model alone guarantees neither capacity nor availability.

clarity.reason: Roles, protocol, API, message parts and session state are defined before applying their limits. Examples do useful work without an artificial recurring story. Shared renderer/CSS inspected once; figure labels/captions match meaning, not runtime-verified behavior.

evidence.quote: Locate persistent application data and any session context separately.

outcomes.reason: All five criteria supported: request initiator/handler roles without browser/hardware constraint; same/different machines and service client role; shared message rules; method/URL/headers/body and response status/headers/content; application-field meanings and errors distinct from response arrival.

All six criteria supported: retained sign-in/session context, A-local dependency and loss; request-carried/shared-retrieved stateless context; replaceable equivalent handlers with remaining storage dependency and authentication; shared centralized behavior/data; network latency/unavailability and overload rejection; no automatic capacity/HA guarantee.

All three criteria supported: generic method/target/input request with interpretation/access/allowed data work and response; separately located durable records and session context; agreed success versus explicit reported error and uncertain no-response including lost success. Operation-specific fields/status/retry implementation are outside conceptual scope.

sourceChecks.claim: Inspected RFC 9110 section 3.3 client/server program roles and same-program multiple-role description, with request/response exchange. Browser and hardware are not defining properties.

Inspected RFC 9110 section 1.3 request intent, target interpretation and status/content semantics plus message field descriptions. OWASP endpoint access controls support rejecting direct unauthorized requests despite hidden client UI.

Inspected Microsoft autoscaling guidance avoiding specific-instance dependency and stateless services. Request-carried/shared context removes local-session dependence while shared storage remains required; no absence-of-data guarantee follows.

Inspected MDN client/server responsibilities, centrally generated/personalized data and optional database-backed work. Network/dependency and capacity tradeoffs follow from distributed request flow; offline-local work requires later shared-state coordination.

Inspected RFC 9110 section 9.2.2 retry after connection failure before response and effect-based idempotency. The original operation may already have succeeded, supporting unknown outcome rather than absence proof.
